definition: Cavort means to leap about, behave boisterously.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word cavort. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know cavort should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The spring lambs cavorted across the pasture, springing sideways at nothing at all.
A skip is one happy bounce in a walk — the smallest, tamest cousin of a cavort.
A romp is energetic, but cavorting is wilder still — add the leaping, the wheeling, and the pleasure in being watched.

Frolic is light, happy play — children splashing in a fountain, a puppy loose in the leaves — gentle fun with no audience in mind. Cavort turns the volume up: bigger leaps, wilder wheeling, and a distinct pleasure in being watched. Frolickers amuse themselves; cavorters half expect applause.

Gambol means to skip and leap playfully, and it is said mostly of lambs, foals, and small children — light-footed, innocent springing. Cavorting is rowdier and showier: not just leaps but tumbling, wheeling, and mugging for the crowd. A lamb gambols in a meadow; a mascot cavorts down a parade.

Because cavort's own parentage is a guess, it built no word family — no prefix, no shared root. If the curvet theory is right, its only relative is that rare riding term, which most dictionaries now file under 'horses, historical.'
Cavort means to leap about, behave boisterously.
Between floats, the costumed mascots cavorted down the parade route — leapfrogging traffic cones, spinning surprised bystanders, high-kicking through the marching band's gaps.
Cavort is bigger than play and bouncier than dance: it is whole-body, look-at-me friskiness — leaping, tumbling, wheeling about.
Animals cavort in fields; children cavort in leaf piles; adults cavort mostly at weddings, and deny it on Monday.
Cavort when the joy is physical and a little showy — bodies in motion, dignity optional.
Frolic is gentler, romp is loose energetic play, and this unit's carouse is the tablebound cousin: carousers sing and pour; cavorters leap and spin.

The harbor's sea lions have learned exactly when the tour boats come by.

At half past ten, as the first deck of tourists rounds the point, the young males begin to cavort: hurling themselves off the pier, corkscrewing through the wake, slapping the water with theatrical smacks.
Marine biologists insist the display serves no purpose — no hunting, no courtship, nothing but commotion.
The sea lions appear unbothered by the science.
When a boat idles, the show grows wilder; when the last boat leaves, it stops almost at once.
Deckhands swear the animals count the cameras.
'No audience, no acrobatics,' one said, shrugging.
'They're hams, plain and simple.'
